Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

UNITED NATIONS (CNN) -- The United Nations humanitarian chief Wednesday criticized a two-day pause in the fighting between the Sri Lankan army and Tamil Tiger rebels as "inadequate." U.N. Nations humanitarian chief John Holmes said he would have liked a "proper humanitarian pause." John Holmes, the under secretary general for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator, told reporters that the 48-hour break in hostilities was not sufficient, even as fighting resumed in the northeast of the country. The brief cessation of hostilities was announced by the Sri Lankan government on April 12 and allowed the U.N. and its partners to bring in necessary aid, said Holmes. He said he would have liked a "proper humanitarian pause" that lasted longer than two days, but hoped the break allowed for some progress to occur. Secretary-General Ban ki-Moon had originally welcomed the announcement by the Sri Lankan government. However, Ban also expressed his concern that, "This is less than the full humanitarian pause of several days I had pressed for." But Ban added that the pause "is nevertheless a useful first step and an opportunity to move towards the peaceful and orderly end to the fighting now so badly needed." The government of Sri Lanka has been battling the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Elam (LTTE) rebels in a civil conflict that has lasted nearly 25 years. The LTTE has been declared a terrorist organization by 32 countries, including the United States and the nations of the European Union. As many as 70,000 people have been killed since the conflict officially began in 1983. The most pressing concern now, according to Holmes, is the fact that over 100,000 people are currently crowded in a "very small pocket of land" that is about five square miles, or about twice the size of New York's Central Park. "It is a very small area indeed for what we believe is very large number of people" Holmes explained. The crowded population, primarily comprised of Tamil civilians, is subject to the continuing Sri Lankan government assaults. The British and French foreign ministers released a joint statement as well on Wednesday, claiming that the LTTE is also using Tamil civilians as human shields. Holmes also called attention to the fact that the press has been barred from covering the civil strife in Sri Lanka. Ultimately, Holmes and the United Nations would like to see a peaceful end to the hostilities, but "its pretty clear, frankly, that a ceasefire as such is not something available at present circumstances."

outputs.L1:
UNITED NATIONS (CNN) — The United Nations’ humanitarian chief on Wednesday criticized a two-day pause in fighting between the Sri Lankan army and Tamil Tiger rebels as “inadequate.”

John Holmes, the U.N. under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator, told reporters that he would have preferred a “proper humanitarian pause.” He said the 48-hour break in hostilities was insufficient, even as fighting resumed in the country’s northeast.

The brief cessation of hostilities, announced by the Sri Lankan government on April 12, allowed the U.N. and its partners to deliver necessary aid, Holmes said. He added that he would have wanted a “proper humanitarian pause” lasting longer than two days, but hoped the break had allowed some progress to be made.

Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon had initially welcomed the Sri Lankan government’s announcement. However, he also expressed concern, saying, “This is less than the full humanitarian pause of several days I had pressed for.” Ban added that the pause “is nevertheless a useful first step and an opportunity to move towards the peaceful and orderly end to the fighting now so badly needed.”

The government of Sri Lanka has been battling the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels in a civil conflict that has lasted nearly 25 years. The LTTE has been designated a terrorist organization by 32 countries, including the United States and the nations of the European Union. As many as 70,000 people have been killed since the conflict officially began in 1983.

The most pressing concern now, according to Holmes, is that more than 100,000 people are crowded into a “very small pocket of land” of about five square miles, roughly twice the size of New York’s Central Park. “It is a very small area indeed for what we believe is a very large number of people,” Holmes explained.

The crowded population, composed primarily of Tamil civilians, remains subject to continuing Sri Lankan government assaults. The British and French foreign ministers also released a joint statement on Wednesday, alleging that the LTTE is using Tamil civilians as human shields.

Holmes also drew attention to the fact that the press has been barred from covering the civil strife in Sri Lanka.

Ultimately, Holmes and the United Nations would like to see a peaceful end to the hostilities, but “it’s pretty clear, frankly, that a ceasefire as such is not something available in the present circumstances.”

UNITED NATIONS (CNN) — On Wednesday, the United Nations’ top humanitarian official said a two-day halt in combat between Sri Lankan government forces and Tamil Tiger rebels was not enough.

John Holmes, the U.N. under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator, told journalists he had hoped for a longer and more substantial “proper humanitarian pause.” He said the 48-hour suspension of fighting was insufficient, particularly as clashes had already restarted in Sri Lanka’s northeast.

Sri Lanka’s government announced the temporary stop in hostilities on April 12, and Holmes said it gave the United Nations and partner organizations a chance to deliver essential assistance. Still, he said he would have preferred a pause lasting more than two days, while adding that he hoped the brief break had allowed at least some progress.

U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon had initially welcomed the Sri Lankan government’s announcement. At the same time, he voiced concern that the measure fell short of “the full humanitarian pause of several days” he had requested. Ban said the pause was nonetheless “a useful first step” and could provide an opening to move toward the peaceful and orderly conclusion to the fighting that was urgently needed.

The Sri Lankan government has been fighting the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, in a civil conflict that has continued for almost 25 years. Thirty-two countries, including the United States and European Union member states, have designated the LTTE as a terrorist group. Since the war formally began in 1983, up to 70,000 people have died.

Holmes said the most urgent problem is that more than 100,000 people are packed into a “very small pocket of land” measuring roughly five square miles — about twice the size of New York’s Central Park. He described it as an extremely limited space for what the U.N. believes is a very large population.

The people crowded into that area, mostly Tamil civilians, remain exposed to ongoing attacks by Sri Lankan government forces. In a joint statement issued Wednesday, the foreign ministers of Britain and France also accused the LTTE of using Tamil civilians as human shields.

Holmes further noted that journalists have not been allowed to report freely on Sri Lanka’s civil conflict. He said that, in the end, both he and the United Nations want the violence to conclude peacefully, but added that “a ceasefire as such” did not appear to be possible under the current circumstances.

Ban had urged the parties to agree to a halt lasting several days, in order to give humanitarian workers enough time to assist civilians and improve conditions on the ground.

He warned that the concentration of so many people in such limited space made the need for humanitarian access even more urgent.

Holmes argued that a much longer humanitarian ceasefire was needed to allow aid agencies to reach civilians, deliver food and medical supplies, evacuate the wounded, and ensure the protection of people trapped by the fighting. While the temporary pause did permit limited relief access, he said it fell far short of what was required given the scale of civilian suffering.

More than 100,000 people remained trapped in a small area where government forces and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam were engaged in intense fighting. Humanitarian officials warned that civilians in the zone faced severe shortages of food, medicine, clean water, and shelter, while also being exposed to the dangers of shelling and crossfire.

The Sri Lankan government described the pause as an opportunity for civilians to leave the conflict area, but U.N. officials and aid groups said the short duration made it difficult to mount an effective humanitarian operation. Holmes emphasized that protecting civilians must be the priority and called for a fuller halt to hostilities so aid workers could operate safely and reach those most in need.

The situation highlighted growing international concern over the final stages of the conflict and the fate of civilians caught between the advancing Sri Lankan military and the Tamil Tiger rebels. Holmes’ criticism underscored the view that a brief suspension of fighting was insufficient and that only a more sustained ceasefire could create the conditions necessary for meaningful humanitarian relief.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about U.N. humanitarian chief John Holmes criticizing Sri Lanka’s 48-hour pause in fighting with the Tamil Tigers as inadequate, including Ban Ki-moon’s reaction and the humanitarian concerns for trapped civilians.
counterfactuals.output:
**U.N. official says Sri Lanka’s 48-hour cease-fire is not enough**

**UNITED NATIONS** — The United Nations’ top humanitarian official criticized Sri Lanka’s 48-hour pause in fighting with Tamil Tiger rebels as inadequate, saying it would not provide enough time to move civilians out of the combat zone or deliver desperately needed aid.

John Holmes, the U.N. under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs, said the brief suspension of military operations fell short of what was needed as tens of thousands of civilians remained trapped in a shrinking area of northeastern Sri Lanka, where government forces were battling the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE.

Holmes said humanitarian workers needed sustained access to civilians caught between the two sides, many of whom were believed to be short of food, medicine and clean water. Aid agencies have warned that shelling, overcrowding and the lack of medical care have created increasingly dire conditions for families unable to flee.

U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon responded cautiously to Sri Lanka’s announcement, welcoming any step that could reduce civilian suffering but urging both the government and the Tamil Tigers to do far more to protect noncombatants.

Ban called on the LTTE to allow civilians to leave the conflict area freely and appealed to the Sri Lankan government to extend humanitarian access and avoid the use of heavy weapons in areas where civilians were present. He also urged a longer pause in the fighting to allow aid deliveries and safe evacuations.

Sri Lankan officials said the 48-hour pause was intended to give civilians time to escape from LTTE-held territory. The government has accused the rebels of using civilians as human shields, a charge the Tigers have denied or disputed in the past.

The LTTE, which has fought for decades for an independent Tamil homeland, has been pushed into a small coastal strip after a major government offensive. As the battlefield has narrowed, international concern has grown over the fate of civilians trapped there.

Holmes said the priority must be the immediate protection of civilians, including the wounded and children, and access for U.N. and other relief agencies.

The United Nations has repeatedly warned that the civilian population is paying the heaviest price in the final stages of the conflict, with hospitals overwhelmed and basic supplies running out. Humanitarian officials said a short pause, without guarantees of safe passage and aid access, would do little to address the scale of the crisis.

counterfactuals.output:
**U.N. Calls for Civilian Protection as Sri Lanka Announces Two-Day Humanitarian Pause**

**United Nations** — The United Nations has urged all sides in Sri Lanka’s civil war to ensure the safety of civilians after the government announced a two-day humanitarian pause in its military offensive against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, in the country’s northeast.

U.N. officials welcomed the temporary halt as a potential opportunity to evacuate the wounded, deliver urgently needed assistance and allow trapped civilians to move to safer areas. But they warned that a pause of only two days would not be enough unless aid workers are granted full access and both the Sri Lankan military and LTTE respect international humanitarian law.

Tens of thousands of civilians are believed to be trapped in a shrinking conflict zone along Sri Lanka’s northeastern coast, where government forces have been advancing against the LTTE in the final stages of a decades-long war. The United Nations has repeatedly expressed concern over reports of heavy civilian casualties, including deaths and injuries caused by shelling in densely populated areas.

The U.N. has also accused the LTTE of preventing civilians from leaving the combat zone, effectively using them as human shields. At the same time, U.N. humanitarian officials have called on the Sri Lankan government to avoid the use of heavy weapons in areas where civilians are concentrated and to allow independent monitoring of conditions on the ground.

Humanitarian agencies say medical supplies, food and clean water are running dangerously low. Makeshift medical facilities have struggled to treat large numbers of wounded civilians, while aid convoys and evacuations have been limited by the fighting.

The crisis has also placed severe pressure on displacement sites in government-controlled areas. Camps in the northeast, particularly in and around Vavuniya, have become overcrowded as civilians flee the conflict zone. U.N. agencies have raised concerns about shelter, sanitation, freedom of movement and the screening of displaced people by Sri Lankan authorities.

U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and senior humanitarian officials have called for a longer humanitarian pause, the safe evacuation of civilians, and full access for aid organizations. They have stressed that civilians must be allowed to leave the conflict zone voluntarily and that displaced people must be treated in accordance with international standards.

The Sri Lankan government has said its operations are aimed at defeating the LTTE and ending terrorism on the island. The LTTE, which fought for an independent Tamil state, had been designated a terrorist organization by several countries.

The war, which lasted more than 25 years, has left deep ethnic and political divisions in Sri Lanka. As fighting intensified in its final phase, the United Nations warned that the civilian population in the northeast faced an increasingly desperate humanitarian emergency.

**U.N. official: Sri Lanka pause not enough to aid trapped civilians**

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka —** The Sri Lankan government’s brief halt in fighting was not sufficient to deliver meaningful help to tens of thousands of civilians trapped between advancing troops and Tamil Tiger rebels, the United Nations’ top humanitarian official said.

John Holmes, the U.N. under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs, said the limited pause in hostilities did not allow aid workers enough time or access to evacuate the wounded, move supplies into the conflict zone or provide protection for civilians caught in the shrinking area held by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam.

Sri Lanka announced the temporary suspension as its military pressed deeper into rebel-held territory in the country’s northeast, where officials said they were nearing the end of a decades-long war. The government said the pause was intended to allow civilians to leave the combat area.

But U.N. officials and aid agencies have warned that many civilians remain unable to escape safely. Holmes said a longer humanitarian pause, with guarantees from both sides, was needed to allow relief operations to reach those most at risk.

The Sri Lankan government has accused the Tamil Tigers of using civilians as human shields and preventing them from leaving. The rebels have denied deliberately endangering civilians and have accused the military of shelling populated areas.

Independent accounts from the conflict zone have been difficult to verify because journalists and most aid organizations have been barred from the front lines.

International pressure has grown as the humanitarian situation has worsened. Aid workers say food, medicine and clean water are in short supply, while makeshift medical facilities are overwhelmed by the number of wounded.

Holmes said the priority must be the safe evacuation of civilians and the delivery of emergency assistance, adding that a short pause in fighting could not address the scale of the crisis.

Sri Lanka’s government has rejected calls for a broader cease-fire, saying it would give the Tigers time to regroup. Officials have insisted the military operation is aimed at rescuing civilians and defeating a group they classify as terrorist.

The Tamil Tigers have fought since the early 1980s for an independent homeland for ethnic Tamils in the north and east of Sri Lanka. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed breaking-news story covering the U.N. criticism of Sri Lanka’s temporary ceasefire, the trapped Tamil civilian population, accusations against the LTTE, and the lack of press access to the conflict zone.
counterfactuals.output:
**U.N. criticizes Sri Lanka’s temporary ceasefire as civilians remain trapped in war zone**

**COLOMBO, Sri Lanka —** The United Nations has criticized Sri Lanka’s temporary ceasefire in its final offensive against the Tamil Tiger rebels, warning that the pause is too limited to protect tens of thousands of civilians trapped in the shrinking conflict zone and calling for urgent access to evacuate the wounded and deliver humanitarian aid.

Sri Lankan authorities announced a brief halt in military operations, describing it as a humanitarian measure intended to allow civilians to leave the fighting area in the island’s northeast. But U.N. officials and aid agencies said the pause did not amount to a full humanitarian ceasefire and was unlikely to be enough to move large numbers of civilians to safety.

The fighting centers on a small strip of territory still held by the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or LTTE, who have been battling for decades to create an independent Tamil homeland in northern and eastern Sri Lanka. Government forces have steadily advanced in recent months, leaving the rebels cornered along with a large civilian population, many of them ethnic Tamils who fled earlier battles and are now trapped between the army’s front lines and Tiger-held areas.

U.N. officials have voiced growing alarm over civilian casualties, shortages of food and medicine, and the inability of aid workers to reach people inside the conflict zone. Humanitarian agencies say makeshift medical facilities have been overwhelmed, with wounded civilians unable to leave and doctors working with dwindling supplies.

At the same time, the United Nations and international rights groups have accused the LTTE of preventing civilians from escaping, effectively using them as human shields. The rebels have also been accused of forcing civilians, including children, into their ranks and firing from positions near populated areas, increasing the danger to noncombatants.

Sri Lanka’s government denies deliberately targeting civilians and says its forces are conducting a “rescue operation” to free people held by the LTTE. Officials argue that the rebels are responsible for the humanitarian crisis because they refuse to surrender and have blocked civilians from crossing into government-held territory.

But the government has faced sharp international criticism over the scale of shelling and the lack of independent access to the battlefield. Journalists have been barred from entering the conflict zone, and most international aid organizations have had only limited or no access. As a result, casualty figures and accounts of conditions inside the war zone are difficult to verify independently.

The absence of press access has heightened concern among diplomats, humanitarian officials and rights monitors, who say both the government and the LTTE are operating with little outside scrutiny. Reports from the area rely heavily on government statements, rebel-linked sources, doctors in the war zone, U.N. contacts and accounts from civilians who have managed to escape.

U.N. officials have urged both sides to protect civilians under international humanitarian law. They have called on the LTTE to allow civilians to leave immediately and on the Sri Lankan government to extend the ceasefire long enough for safe evacuations, medical assistance and the delivery of relief supplies.

The crisis marks one of the most dangerous phases of Sri Lanka’s long civil war. The LTTE, once a powerful guerrilla and conventional fighting force with a navy and a de facto administration, has lost nearly all of its territory. The government says the war is close to an end, but humanitarian officials warn that the final stage could bring catastrophic consequences for civilians unless both sides agree to a broader pause in fighting and allow independent access to the area.

International pressure on Colombo is increasing, with calls for a durable humanitarian ceasefire, transparency in military operations and protection for displaced civilians moving into government-run camps. Sri Lankan officials have rejected outside demands that they say could give the LTTE time to regroup, insisting the military campaign will continue until the rebels are defeated.

For civilians trapped in the war zone, the temporary ceasefire has offered only a narrow and uncertain window of safety. Aid agencies warn that without a longer halt in fighting and secure evacuation routes, thousands remain at risk from shelling, crossfire, hunger and untreated injuries.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
UNITED NATIONS (CNN) -- The United Nations humanitarian chief said Monday that a 48-hour pause in fighting in Sri Lanka was inadequate to meet the urgent needs of civilians trapped in the country’s northern war zone and called for a longer humanitarian halt to the conflict.

John Holmes, the U.N. under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs, said the pause announced by the Sri Lankan government would not provide enough time to evacuate the wounded, deliver sufficient food and medicine, or allow civilians to move safely out of the combat area.

Tens of thousands of people have been caught between advancing government forces and the rebel Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam, or Tamil Tigers, in a shrinking strip of territory along Sri Lanka’s northeast coast. U.N. officials and aid agencies have warned that food, clean water and medical supplies are running dangerously low.

Holmes urged both the Sri Lankan military and the Tamil Tigers to agree to a longer pause in hostilities and to allow aid workers full access to civilians. He also called on the rebels to let civilians leave the conflict zone freely, saying noncombatants must not be used as human shields.

Sri Lanka’s government has said its offensive is aimed at defeating the Tamil Tigers, who have fought for decades for a separate Tamil homeland. The government has rejected calls for a permanent cease-fire, arguing that the rebels would use it to regroup.

U.N. officials have said that any humanitarian pause must be long enough and secure enough to permit large-scale relief operations and medical evacuations. The United Nations has repeatedly expressed concern over civilian casualties as the fighting has intensified.
